Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A black-capped chickadee perched on a curved autumn branch, with four orange and gold leaves, in a misty blue-gray and orange forest with a low sun

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

19 stepsCanvas: 14 x 11 inFocal point: the chickadee's head and black bib, a little left of center near the top Light: the low sun at the upper right, so lit edges face up and to the rightHow this lesson was made

What you need

Tubes

  • Titanium white
  • Yellow deep
  • Flesh tint
  • Crimson
  • Purple red
  • Violet
  • Ultramarine
  • Light olive green
  • Raw umber
  • Permanent black

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: Blend the misty sunset skyFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #8 round: Paint the sunRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 3/4 inch flat: Pull down the far trunksFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • old stiff flat: Dab the hazy autumn foliageOld stiff flat: worn, splayed bristles, for rough texture like grass and foliage
  • 1/2 inch flat: Paint the branch and trunk darkFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #6 round: Paint the red in the leavesRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 1/2 inch filbert: Block in the bodyFilbert: flat with a rounded end, for soft-edged shapes
  • #2 round: Stripe the wing feathersRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 1/4 inch flat: Soften the cap's edgesFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • liner: Paint the legs and toesLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass

Also

  • A 14 x 11 in canvas, landscape (hang it that way), and masking tape to mark halves and quarters along its edges.
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Your paints

Every paint in the lesson. You don't have to mix them all at the start: each step lists the paints it uses with their recipes, so you can mix a little as you go before it dries. Parts are by volume.

Before you start

Mark halves and quarters on tape

Run a strip of masking tape along the top edge of the canvas and one down a side, and mark the middle and the quarters on each. On your 14 x 11 in canvas the marks across the top are 3 1/2 in apart and the marks down the side 2 3/4 in apart. Every step's Where picture has the same lines, so you can find its place on your canvas. (Chalk lines on the canvas would be painted over by the first coat; the tape stays.)

The transfer outline (optional)

The outlines of the main shapes, on the same quarter grid as your tape: 1 The four leaves; 2 The chickadee. Before the stage that starts one, you can lightly chalk its outline on the canvas, using the tape marks to place it.

Strokes to try on scrap paper first

Each one's card is open in the step that first uses it.

  • X stroke, first in step 1.
  • Small circles, first in step 2.
  • Dry brush, first in step 3. Try it on scrap paper first: wipe the brush until it leaves broken marks.
  • Dabbing, first in step 4.
  • Thick to thin, first in step 5.
  • Press and lift, first in step 9. Try a row of them on scrap paper first.
  • Building from pieces, first in step 11.
  • Curved strokes, first in step 13.
  • Liner work, first in step 18. Try a few lines on scrap paper first.

The basics

Before you start not checked yet

Before you start

Not checked yet

  • Two water jars: one to rinse the brush, one kept clean for thinning paint. A big clear jar shows when the rinse water is dirty.
  • A rag or paper towel, to wipe the brush between colors.
  • Put out bigger puddles of paint than you think you need. Big puddles stay wet longer than small smears.
  • Lay your colors out the same way every time, so they're easy to find and don't get dragged into each other.
Keep your colors clean not checked yet

Keep your colors clean

Not checked yet

  • Wipe the brush on a rag between colors.
  • Rinse it fully before going into white.
  • Rinse often. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  • Mix on the palette, not on the canvas. Two or three colors at most: stop when the color is right.
Colors dry darker not checked yet

Colors dry darker

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic looks lighter when wet than when dry.
  • Before a big area, paint a test swatch and let it dry before judging the mix.
Fixing a mistake not checked yet

Fixing a mistake

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic is forgiving. Let the area dry, then paint over it and try again.
  • Don't keep working a spot that's half dry. Leave it, work somewhere else, and come back.
Keep paint from drying on the palette not checked yet

Keep paint from drying on the palette

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic on a brushstroke stays wet for only a few minutes.
  • Mist the palette lightly with a spray bottle now and then. Only lightly: too much water weakens the paint.
  • Cover the paint when you aren't using it.
Let each layer dry not checked yet

Let each layer dry

Not checked yet

  • Between steps, the paint underneath should be dry to the touch. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  • Painting into half-dry paint drags it up and turns it gooey and muddy.
  • Thick paint can feel dry on top and still be wet inside. Give thick areas longer.
  • Fine lines and light colors over dark especially need a dry layer underneath.
Light colors over dark need more than one coat not checked yet

Light colors over dark need more than one coat

Not checked yet

  • One coat of white or a light color over a dark one usually looks gray and patchy.
  • Expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry. Use the paint thick, with little water.
Making a color lighter or darker not checked yet

Making a color lighter or darker

Not checked yet

  • To lighten: add the color to the white a little at a time, not white to the color.
  • White also dulls a color. Too much turns it chalky.
  • To darken: add the dark into the lighter mix in small amounts.
  • For the next lighter value of something, start from the mix you already have and add white, so the colors stay related.
One light direction not checked yet

One light direction

Not checked yet

  • Pick where the light comes from and put every highlight on that side.
  • Each thing is built the same way: the whole shape in a darker or middle value, a lighter value on the side facing the light, then the lightest on a small area at the very edge. Each covers less than the one before.
The ugly stage not checked yet

The ugly stage

Not checked yet

  • Partway through, every painting looks flat or wrong. That's normal. Keep building.
  • Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.
  • Details come last, and only on shapes that are already right.
How much water not checked yet

How much water

Not checked yet

  • Keep water to about half the mix or less. More than that makes weak, see-through color that can lift when you paint over it.
  • For covering, use the paint thick, with little or no water.
  • After rinsing, wipe the metal part of the brush dry.

The misty sky 2 steps

STEP 1 OF 19 · The misty sky, 1 of 2

Blend the misty sunset sky

  1. Inside the outlined area: the whole canvas.
  2. Paints, top to bottom: Warm apricot, then Misty lavender-gray.
  3. Mix enough Warm apricot for this step and steps 4, 7, 9 and 11; cover it between them.
  4. Mix enough Misty lavender-gray for this step and steps 8 and 12; cover it between them.
  5. Brush: 1 inch flat. Load: One or two colors on the brush. How much of each is on it controls the blend.
  6. Short strokes that cross each other in two directions, like overlapping X shapes.
  7. It should leave a soft, slightly textured blended fill with visible criss-cross marks.

Tip: The light comes from the low sun in the upper right, so every highlight in this painting goes on the upper-right side of things. Keep the apricot warm and strongest around the sun's spot (about 9 1/2 in from the left, 1 1/2 in down) and let it melt into lavender-gray toward the left and bottom edges. Colors dry a little darker, so test each mix on the palette edge first. The thin brown sliver at the lower left in the picture is the underside of the branch; skip it, the branch step paints it.

STEP 2 OF 19 · The misty sky, 2 of 2

Paint the sun

  1. Let the misty sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush fully first: this is the lightest paint yet.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 1 in from the top edge, and its right side is about 4 in from the right edge; it's about 1 1/4 in wide and 1 1/4 in tall.
  4. Paint: Sun cream.
  5. Brush: #8 round.
  6. Paint the sun with small circles of the brush tip, starting in its middle and working round and round outward to the edge.
  7. It should leave a bumpy, soft edge.
  8. Watch out: the edge is too hard. Fix: soften it with lighter circular passes of the same paint.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: The sun is a circle a little over an inch across, centered about 9 1/2 in from the left edge and 1 1/2 in down. Keep its edge soft so it glows into the apricot around it.

The far woods 2 steps

STEP 3 OF 19 · The far woods, 1 of 2

Pull down the far trunks

  1. Let the misty sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area, top to bottom to the right edge. Its left side is about 3 in from the right edge.
  4. Paint: Hazy blue-gray.
  5. Mix enough Hazy blue-gray for this step and step 4; cover it between them.
  6. Brush: 3/4 inch flat. Load: A dry brush, no water. Load only the tip, then wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel. It should feel dry and hard to apply.
  7. Light pressure, skimming the surface.
  8. It leaves feathery, see-through marks at first. Build it up in several light passes until each trunk reads as a soft, misty band, as in the Result picture.
  9. Watch out: It went on solid. The brush was too loaded. Fix: let it dry, then dry-brush the base color back over part of it.

Tip: Two tall trunks run the full height on the right, with a shorter fainter one beside them, as the Where picture shows. Pull every stroke straight down, top to bottom, and keep the edges soft and misty.

STEP 4 OF 19 · The far woods, 2 of 2

Dab the hazy autumn foliage

  1. Let the far misty trunks and the misty sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. It reaches all four edges of the canvas.
  3. Paints, darkest first: Hazy blue-gray, then Warm apricot. The paint map shows where each goes.
  4. Brush: old stiff flat. Load: Little paint, fairly dry.
  5. Tap with the tip of the brush. The more you tap one spot, the more solid it gets.
  6. It should leave dots or dappled patches that get more solid the more you tap.
  7. Watch out: Blobs instead of dots. The brush is too wet or holds too much paint. Fix: wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel and tap again.
  8. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Dab the Hazy blue-gray first: a few soft upright trunk shapes on the left and in the middle, and some patches near the top left. Then dab the apricot in loose clumps, thickest around the sun and in the upper right, with a few clumps low on the left and along the bottom. Leave plenty of the misty gray showing between them; the soft gaps make it look far away.

The branch 4 steps

STEP 5 OF 19 · The branch, 1 of 4

Paint the branch and trunk dark

  1. Let the far woods and the misty sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area. It reaches all four edges of the canvas.
  4. Paint: Bark brown.
  5. Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
  6. Press the full width of the flat for the thick trunk and branch, then turn onto its edge and lighten the pressure as you pull out to the twig tips.
  7. It should leave a stroke that starts wide and tapers to a point, so the trunk is thick and the twigs end in points.

Tip: The trunk rises from the bottom-left corner and up the left side, and the branch leaves it about 3 in up from the bottom, arching across to its high point near the middle (about 4 1/2 in from the top) and dipping down to thin twigs at the right. Pull each stroke along the branch, thick at the trunk end and thinner toward the twigs. The picture shows a few dark bumps on top of the branch and around the right-hand twigs; step 8 turns them back into misty gray, so you can leave them out. The painting can look rough at this point; that's the ugly stage, and it's normal.

STEP 6 OF 19 · The branch, 2 of 4

Drag bark tan along the branch

  1. Let the branch and the far woods dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area, all the way across from the top edge. Its bottom is about 1/4 in from the bottom edge.
  3. Paint: Bark tan.
  4. Brush: 1/2 inch flat. Load: A dry brush, no water. Load only the tip, then wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel. It should feel dry and hard to apply.
  5. Light pressure, skimming the surface.
  6. It should leave feathery, broken, see-through marks that catch the canvas texture. Never a solid area.
  7. Leave what step 5 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Watch out: It went on solid. The brush was too loaded. Fix: let it dry, then dry-brush the base color back over part of it.

Tip: Drag the tan in short strokes along the length of the branch and up the trunk, mostly along the middle and the lower side of the branch. Keep plenty of the dark brown showing between the strokes.

STEP 7 OF 19 · The branch, 3 of 4

Catch the sunlight on the bark

  1. Let the branch and the far woods dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area, all the way across from the top edge. Its bottom is about 1/4 in from the bottom edge.
  3. Paint: Warm apricot.
  4. Brush: 1/2 inch flat. Load: A dry brush, no water. Load only the tip, then wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel. It should feel dry and hard to apply.
  5. Light pressure, skimming the surface.
  6. It should leave feathery, broken, see-through marks that catch the canvas texture. Never a solid area.
  7. Leave what steps 5 and 6 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Warm apricot is much lighter than what it goes over: expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry.
  9. Watch out: It went on solid. The brush was too loaded. Fix: let it dry, then dry-brush the base color back over part of it.

Tip: The sun is up and to the right, so the light sits on the top of the branch and the right side of the trunk. Skim the apricot only along those edges, and leave the underside dark.

The leaves 2 steps

STEP 9 OF 19 · The leaves, 1 of 2

Block in the four leaves

  1. Let the branch and the far woods dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, placed with the tape marks.
  3. Inside the outlined area, top to bottom to the right edge. Its left side is about 1 in from the left edge.
  4. Paint: Warm apricot.
  5. Brush: #8 round. Load: Paint loaded well into the belly of the brush, creamy, not runny.
  6. Touch down with the tip, press so the belly spreads, then pull and lift so the stroke ends on the tip.
  7. Each stroke leaves one teardrop-shaped lobe, wide where you pressed and pointed where you lifted; a few of them together make one leaf.
  8. Watch out: A blob instead of a teardrop. Too much paint, or too slow a lift. Fix: use less paint and lift faster.

Tip: Two leaves hang at the top left, one near the top edge and one just below it by the trunk, and two hang below the branch on the right, from a thin stem. Each leaf is a pointed maple shape: build it from a few press-and-lift lobes fanned out from where the stem joins, points outward.

The feet 2 steps

STEP 18 OF 19 · The feet, 1 of 2

Paint the legs and toes

  1. Let the chickadee's body and the branch dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.

  3. Paint: Chickadee black.
  4. Brush: liner. Load: Thin the paint with water until it flows like ink: swirl the brush in water, then in the paint. Reload often.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: a black-capped chickadee perched on a curved brown branch, with orange and gold autumn leaves hanging from it, against a soft blue-gray and orange misty forest with a low sun at the upper right

Found in the image: just the picture (an AI-made painting, 900x600, no bars, borders, captions or text)

Done: none

Why: everything in the image is part of the scene

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 14 x 11 in (11x14, landscape)

Done: crop

Left out: about 15%: a thin strip of misty background and the trunk's far left edge on the left, and the twig tip and far right trunk on the right

Why: fit-canvas picked a free crop: the photo is 3:2 and the canvas 14:11, so about 7.5% comes off each side while the bird, branch, leaves and sun all stay whole

Beginner version

What made it too busy: no tiny separate things (no houses, people, posts); the background forest is already loose dabs and soft vertical trunk shapes, one repeated mark; the bark is loose strokes; parts at different distances (haze, far trunks, foliage dabs, near trunk and branch, bird, leaves, twigs) fit max_parts 8 once grouped

Why: the picture is already a loose, impressionist painting at beginner scale, so there is nothing to drop or merge

A small chickadee on a curved branch against a soft, misty autumn wood with a low sun. What matters is the bird's crisp black cap and bib and white cheek against the soft background, and the warm-cool contrast of apricot foliage over lavender-gray mist. The hard parts for a beginner are keeping the background soft and far away, and giving the round little bird its light side without fussing. The lesson should be about painting a soft background straight through, then laying crisp shapes on top of it.

Subject: A black-capped chickadee perched on a curved autumn branch, with four orange and gold leaves, in a misty blue-gray and orange forest with a low sun
Focal point: the chickadee's head and black bib, a little left of center near the top
Light: the low sun at the upper right, so lit edges face up and to the right

What it saw, back to front

  1. Misty sunset sky
  2. The branch
  3. The four leaves
  4. The chickadee
  5. Legs and feet
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front
ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

Paint-along back to front is the owner's pick for acrylic beginners (docs/decisions.md), and it fits this picture: a soft blended misty background painted straight through, then the branch, leaves and bird on top of it.

Passed onacrylic-block-in-beginner

starts from a toned ground and a separate block-in, which the owner's paint-along tutorials skip; the owner chose paint-along for acrylic

How the paint recipes were worked out13 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

  • Misty lavender-gray Delta E 1.5
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts white, 2 parts permanent black, a touch of violet

  • Sun cream Delta E 1.0
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 4 parts white, 1 part yellow deep, a touch of purple red

  • Hazy blue-gray Delta E 1.4
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 2 parts white, 1 part ultramarine, 1 part raw umber, a touch of permanent black

  • Warm apricot Delta E 1.5
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts white, 2 parts yellow deep, 2 parts purple red

Why the steps go in this order19 steps

Back to front: the misty sky blend first, straight through where everything else goes, then the sun, the far trunks and the hazy foliage on it. Then the branch (dark, mid, light, then the cool gray that cleans its edge), the leaves that hang from it, and the bird on top: body and wing coats, the chest light, the wing stripes, the black cap and bib, the cheek, the soft edges with the eye and beak, and the feet last because they wrap over the branch.

  1. 1. Blend the misty sunset sky

    The whole canvas first, blended wet in one go, so the haze is continuous behind everything.

  2. 2. Paint the sun

    The sun sits in the sky, so it goes on as soon as the sky is dry, before anything in front of it.

  3. 3. Pull down the far trunks

    The far trunks are the farthest shapes on the sky; soft and blue-gray so they stay back.

  4. 4. Dab the hazy autumn foliage

    The hazy foliage clumps sit in front of the far trunks and behind the branch, so they come next, dabbed loosely over the dry sky.

  5. 5. Paint the branch and trunk dark

    The branch is the nearest big shape behind the bird; its dark base goes on first so the lighter bark can go over it.

  6. 6. Drag bark tan along the branch

    The middle bark tone builds the texture on the dark base, before the light.

  7. 7. Catch the sunlight on the bark

    The sunlit top edges come after the middle tone, on the sun's side.

  8. 8. Add the cool gray on the bark

    The cool gray rounds the bark and covers the leftover bumps, finishing the branch before the leaves and bird go over it.

  9. 9. Block in the four leaves

    The leaves hang from the finished branch; a flat apricot base for all four first.

  10. 10. Paint the red in the leaves

    The red goes over the dry gold base, mostly on the two red leaves.

  11. 11. Block in the body

    The bird is nearest of all, so it's blocked in once the branch and leaves are done, as one flat warm shape.

  12. 12. Block in the wing and tail

    The gray wing and tail go over the body's coat as their own flat shape.

  13. 13. Light the chest

    The cream light on the chest faces the sun; it goes over the dry body coat, with the shoulder gray.

  14. 14. Stripe the wing feathers

    The dark feather stripes go over the dry gray wing.

  15. 15. Paint the black cap and bib

    The black cap and bib go on over the head's coat once it's dry.

  16. 16. Paint the white cheek

    The white cheek sits between the cap and bib, so it comes right after them.

  17. 17. Soften the cap's edges

    Softening the black edges and adding the eye and beak are the head's last touches.

  18. 18. Paint the legs and toes

    The feet wrap over the branch, so they go on near the end, over both bird and branch.

  19. 19. Catch the light on the toes

    The light on the toes is the last, smallest highlight.

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • outline: 4 runs. foliage needed colors_in/colors_out from part-colors (its points kept taking the blue-gray haze); the sky still claims some soft orange dabs, so those go on in the sky blend. branch (thin) after 2 fix rounds still takes a few blue-gray background blobs above the branch near the feet and around the right twigs; kept as the best outline (a main part can't be dropped). bird-wing needed colors_in/colors_out to take the light gray shoulder from the bird body.
  • paints --add foliage found no second distinct foliage color (Delta E 7.9), so the foliage is one dabbing step with Hazy blue-gray then Warm apricot; the first plan's separate blue-gray pass changed almost nothing.
  • paints --add bird (after the review flagged the belly's buff shading) gave Soft dove gray #a09496, the shoulder gray, not a belly shadow. That made 11 base mixes, over the target of 10; paints kept it as an added paint. Its own pass changed almost nothing, so it was folded into the chest step.
  • Card lines rewritten for this subject: small-circles (cloud wording, on a sun), dry-brush result (never solid, on far trunks that are soft bands), thick-to-thin (angle brush and grass, on a trunk and branch), press-and-lift result (one lobe of a leaf), build-from-pieces (generic oval and ( ) pieces, on the body, wing, cap and cheek), curved-strokes (pumpkin ribs, on a bird's chest), liner (branches, on bird legs). The coats line on cap-edge was dropped (a few dry-brush marks, not a covering coat).
  • The eye and beak are too small to outline; they first show in the cap-edge step (the bird-head part's last pass), so that step's tip names them.
  • No 'colors dry darker' or 'ugly stage' line was drafted by draft-text; they went into the tips of step 1 and step 5.
  • The render SDK needed OPENAI_API_KEY set in the environment even though the proxy supplies the real key; a placeholder value was passed on the command line for each render.
